In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[differential geometry]] a '''Liouville surface'''<ref>{{harvnb|Liouville|1846}}</ref> (named after [[Joseph Liouville]]) is a type of [[surface (differential geometry)|surface]] which in [[local coordinates]] may be written as a [[graph of a function|graph]] in [[Euclidean space|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>]]

:<math>z=f(x,y)</math>

such that the [[first fundamental form]] is of the form

:<math>ds^2 = \big(f_1(x) + f_2(y)\big)\left(dx^2+dy^2\right).</math>

Sometimes a [[metric tensor|metric]] of this form is called a '''Liouville metric'''.  Every [[surface of revolution]] is a Liouville surface.

[[Jean-Gaston Darboux|Darboux]]<ref>{{harvardnb|Darboux|1894}}, §§583-584</ref> gives a general treatment of such surfaces considering a two-dimensional
space <math>(u,v)</math> with metric
:<math>ds^2 = (U-V)(U_1^2\,du^2 + V_1^2\,dv^2),</math>
where <math>U</math> and <math>U_1</math> are functions of <math>u</math> and
<math>V</math> and <math>V_1</math> are functions of <math>v</math>.  A
[[geodesic|geodesic line]] on such a surface is given by
:<math>
\frac{U_1\,du}{\sqrt{U-\alpha}} - \frac{V_1\,dv}{\sqrt{\alpha-V}} = 0
</math>
and the distance along the geodesic is given by
:<math>
ds = \frac{UU_1\,du}{\sqrt{U-\alpha}} - \frac{VV_1\,dv}{\sqrt{\alpha-V}}.
</math>
Here <math>\alpha</math> is a constant related to the direction of the geodesic
by
:<math>
\alpha = U\sin^2\omega + V\cos^2\omega,
</math>
where <math>\omega</math> is the angle of the geodesic measured from a line of constant <math>v</math>.
In this way, the solution of geodesics on Liouville surfaces is reduced to [[Quadrature (differential equations)|quadrature]].
This was first demonstrated by [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi|Jacobi]] for the case of
[[Geodesics on an ellipsoid#Geodesics on a triaxial ellipsoid|geodesics on a triaxial ellipsoid]],<ref>{{harvardnb|Jacobi|1839}}</ref>
a special case of a Liouville surface.
